solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Pam’s disco dancing is somewhat erratic

indicators.note: dancers move about the floor, so the letters are set moving into a new order

blocks.note: the nine letters of the name, its possessive S and the venue, taken as written

explanation.surface: Pam's dancing at the disco is a bit all over the place.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-S looks like grammar but supplies a needed letter. SPASMODIC is the anagram of PAMS DISCO.
explanation.definitionFit: Something spasmodic comes in fits and irregular bursts, so it is a near synonym for being rather unpredictable.

clue.text: Worked hard, putting aside pounds deposited in the bank

indicators.note: to put something aside is to set it apart and drop it, so a letter is taken out

blocks.note: to slave is to toil
L, from Latin libra, is the abbreviation for pounds sterling

explanation.surface: Someone toiled away and banked their earnings instead of spending them.
explanation.walkthrough: SLAVED loses its L to leave SAVED. 'Putting aside' reads as saving money, which is really the definition's job, not the indicator's.
explanation.definitionFit: Money put into a bank account is money kept back for later, which is the ordinary financial sense of the word.

clue.text: Entertainment venue playing REM etc ad nauseam?

indicators.note: a band playing a set performs it in its own way, so the letters are performed in a new arrangement

blocks.note: the band name, the abbreviation and the Latin phrase, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A venue that plays the band R.E.M. and similar acts over and over until you are sick of them.
explanation.walkthrough: R.E.M. is an American rock band, which makes 'playing' look like music. The fifteen letters of REM ETC AD NAUSEAM rearrange to AMUSEMENT ARCADE.
explanation.definitionFit: An amusement arcade is a hall of coin-operated games and machines, a place people visit for fun.

clue.text: Mum overcomes Jack in honourable, good golf game

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it
in a down entry, to come over something is to sit above it, so this piece goes first

blocks.note: a familiar word for mother
Hon is the standard abbreviation used in titles
J is jack in a pack of cards
G is the usual abbreviation for good
G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Mum beats Jack at a gentlemanly, sporting round of golf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Golf game' tempts you to look for a sport, but golf is just a letter from the phonetic alphabet. 'Overcomes' works because this is a down entry, where the first piece sits on top.
explanation.definitionFit: Mah-jongg is a Chinese game played with tiles, usually by four players, so it is a straightforward example of a game.

clue.text: Delicate shot racket struck at the finish

indicators.note: the finish of a word is its very end, so only its closing letter is kept

blocks.note: a racket is a loud noise
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A tennis player plays a soft shot that the racket hits at the end of a rally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racket' and 'shot' set up a tennis scene, but the racket is noise. DIN plus K gives DINK.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis and similar games, a dink is a soft, gently lobbed shot that drops just over the net.

clue.text: Ape gets ringing noise outside tank — runs away

indicators.note: something sent away is no longer there, so it is dropped from the word
to be outside something is to surround it on both sides

blocks.note: a chime is the ring of a bell
a German armoured tank
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: An ape hears a clanging tank and bolts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs away' reads as the ape fleeing, but it is an instruction: the runs letter leaves the tank before the ringing noise goes round it.
explanation.definitionFit: The chimpanzee is one of the great apes of Africa, so it is a plain example of the broader category.

clue.text: Go on to gatecrash very pathetic party

indicators.note: a gatecrasher pushes into an event uninvited, so one piece forces its way inside another

blocks.note: so means very, as in 'so tired'
to go on speaking is to add, as in 'she added'

explanation.surface: Somebody urges you to crash a really dismal party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' looks like a gathering, but in the old legal and colloquial sense it means a person, so 'pathetic party' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Saddo is British slang for a pitiable, socially inept person, and a party can mean an individual person.

clue.text: Only fish landlady gutted

indicators.note: to gut something is to take out its insides, so only the outer letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: a sole is a flatfish
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: The landlady has only one job: cleaning the fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' fits the fish in the surface, but it works on the landlady. SOLE plus LY gives SOLELY.
explanation.definitionFit: Solely and only are synonymous adverbs, both meaning exclusively or with nothing else involved.

clue.text: Drink with retired setter maybe after installing old copper insulator

indicators.note: to install something is to fit it inside, so one piece is put into another

blocks.note: a draught is a gulp of drink
ex means former, as of someone who has left a post
a crossword setter is one who writes clues
D was the abbreviation for the old penny, a copper coin before decimal money

explanation.surface: Someone has a drink with a retired setter (dog) after a retired policeman has moved in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' suggests the dog and 'copper' a policeman; here they are a crossword setter, one who clues, and the old penny of pre-1971 British money.
explanation.definitionFit: A draught excluder is a strip or long cushion laid along a door to stop cold air, so it insulates a room.

clue.text: Oscar winner Charles’s cycling assault

indicators.note: something cycling goes round and round, so letters from the end come round to the front

blocks.note: Charles Laughton won the Best Actor Oscar in 1933, plus the possessive S

explanation.surface: A film star is attacked while out riding his bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' suggests a bike ride; it moves the last three letters of LAUGHTONS to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: An onslaught is a fierce, sustained attack, so it is a direct synonym for an assault.

clue.text: Up with the lark? He’s famous for it!

definitions.text: Up with the lark? He’s famous for it!

blocks.note: surface reading: being up with the lark means rising very early in the morning
setter's reading: a lark going up is a lark ascending, the title of a much-loved English piece for violin and orchestra, and he is the composer famous for it

explanation.surface: A famously early riser is known for getting up at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for early rising hides 'The Lark Ascending' (1914), Ralph Vaughan Williams's best-known work.
explanation.definitionFit: Vaughan Williams was the English composer of The Lark Ascending, and his fame rests largely on that piece.

clue.text: Wanderer heading west loaded with Eastern spirit

indicators.note: in an across entry west is leftward, so the letters run from right to left
something loaded with cargo carries it inside

blocks.note: a nomad has no fixed home
E is the abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A traveller goes west carrying a spirit from the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eastern spirit' reads as a phrase, but 'Eastern' is only the letter E. NOMAD turned round is DAMON, and E goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A daemon is a supernatural being or inner guiding genius in Greek thought, so it is a variant word for a spirit.

clue.text: Mint in silver wrapping I ate at the outset as defence

indicators.note: wrapping goes round a present, so one piece surrounds another
the outset is the beginning, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
Polo is a British brand of mint sweet with a hole in the middle
taken as written
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone excuses eating a sweet that came in silver foil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mint' looks like a verb or freshness; it is a Polo, the British mint with a hole, and silver is its chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: An apologia is a formal written defence of one's opinions or conduct, as in Newman's Apologia Pro Vita Sua.

clue.text: Hotshot lawyer on mag finally getting stuck into a couple of beers

indicators.note: finally points to the end of the word, so only its last letter is used
something stuck into another thing is lodged inside it

blocks.note: in cricket the on side is also called the leg side
two ales, one after the other
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A star barrister appears in a magazine after a couple of pints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' looks like a joining word, but it is the cricket term. LEG comes first, then G is lodged inside the second of the two ALEs.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal eagle is an informal idiom for a sharp, highly successful lawyer, so it matches a hotshot in that profession.

clue.text: Such as The Hollies’ perennial hits?

blocks.note: first meaning: plants such as hollies keep their leaves all year
second meaning: songs that stay popular year after year

explanation.walkthrough: The Hollies were a 1960s British pop group, so the surface is about their lasting hits; the capitals are surface dressing, and holly bushes are the first sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Hollies are plants that keep green leaves through winter, and songs that never date are called by the same horticultural word.

clue.text: Where unchallenged professor might relax?

blocks.note: something unchallenging is easy
a professor holds a chair, the title of a senior university post

explanation.surface: A professor whose position faces no threat can put their feet up.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, and its two key words also build the answer: an untroubled professorship is an easy chair.
explanation.definitionFit: An easy chair is a large comfortable armchair, exactly the place where anyone sits back and unwinds.

clue.text: One aiming at a fast buck or deer

definitions.text: One aiming at a fast buck

blocks.clueFragment: One aiming at a fast buck
blocks.note: first meaning: a speculator who buys new shares hoping to sell them quickly at a profit
second meaning: a male deer

explanation.surface: A hunter takes aim at a running buck or some other deer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buck' looks like a male deer, matching the second meaning, but here it is slang for money. Stag is a stock-market term.
explanation.definitionFit: On the stock exchange a speculator subscribing to new issues for quick resale is so called, and the word also names an adult male deer.

clue.text: Bevan almost succeeded to get on top of mass disorder

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is left off
in a down entry, being on top means being placed above, so this piece comes before the next

blocks.note: Aneurin Bevan, the Welsh Labour minister who founded the NHS
S is the abbreviation for succeeded in genealogies
M is the symbol for mass in physics

explanation.surface: A politician nearly managed to get a grip on mass unrest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass disorder' reads as a riot; 'disorder' is the medical definition. ANEURIN minus N, then S above M.
explanation.definitionFit: An aneurism (also spelt aneurysm) is a dangerous swelling of an artery wall, a medical condition.

clue.text: Earth to become fine with time

blocks.note: weather that sets fair becomes settled and fine
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: The ground gets better as time passes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earth' looks like soil or the planet, but it is an animal's burrow. 'Become fine' is a loose route to SET, through the weather phrase 'set fair'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sett is a badger's burrow, and an earth is the general hunting term for a burrowing animal's home.

clue.text: Leave, having failed intake exam

indicators.note: something that has failed has broken down, so the letters fall apart and are rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A student quits school after failing the entrance test.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pairs failing an exam with leaving; the ten letters of INTAKE EXAM rearrange into the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To make an exit is an idiom for departing, especially from a room or stage, so it means to go away.

clue.text: Follow us heading north in unspoiled surroundings

indicators.note: in a down entry north is upward, so the letters read from bottom to top
surroundings lie all around something, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: unspoiled means untainted
taken as written

explanation.surface: An invitation to travel north with us through unspoilt countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading north' only reverses because this is a down entry, which reads upward when turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: To pursue is to chase or go after someone, which is a standard synonym for follow.

clue.text: Fairground Attraction song adopting American English

indicators.note: to adopt is to take into the family, so one piece is taken inside another

blocks.note: a carol is a song, especially at Christmas
US is the abbreviation for American
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Fairground Attraction, the British band behind 'Perfect', record a song in American English.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make it look like the band name; read in lower case it is a fairground ride, and capitals carry no wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A carousel is a merry-go-round, the classic revolving ride found at any funfair or travelling show.

clue.text: Mathematician prompt to withdraw cover

indicators.note: to withdraw is to draw back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a cue prompts an actor
a lid covers a pot

explanation.surface: A mathematician is urged to take back his cover story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prompt' looks like an adjective meaning quick; it is the noun for an actor's signal, and 'to withdraw' turns it back.
explanation.definitionFit: Euclid was the Greek geometer of Alexandria whose Elements founded classical geometry, an example of the class named.

clue.text: Attract Liberal, in a manner of speaking

blocks.note: to draw a crowd is to attract it
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A politician wins over a Liberal, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a manner of speaking' reads as the hedge 'so to speak', but the definition is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawl is a slow, lengthened way of talking, so it is one particular style of speech.

clue.text: Carve cross, removing each end

indicators.note: removing both ends strips off the first and last letters

blocks.note: cross means irritable

explanation.surface: An instruction to carve a cross without its ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like a shape to carve, but it is the adjective for bad-tempered.
explanation.definitionFit: To etch is to cut a design into a surface, so it is a close synonym for carve.

clue.text: Raj account switching deposits again into Agra’s banks

indicators.note: switching things round changes their places, so the letters are reordered
a river's banks are its edges, so only the outside letters are used
going into something means being placed inside it

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the city name
taken as written

explanation.surface: A banker in the days of British rule moves money between Agra's banks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Account' and 'banks' suggest finance; the account is a story and the banks are the outer letters of Agra. The Raj was British rule in India.
explanation.definitionFit: A Passage to India is E. M. Forster's 1924 novel set in British India, so it is a fictional narrative of that era.

clue.text: Ruff partner, always reflecting when holding spade finally

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror appears the other way round
finally points to the end of the word, so only its last letter is used
to hold something is to have it inside

blocks.note: ever means always, as in 'ever hopeful'
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A bridge player trumps with a spade, which is always reflected in the partnership's play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruff' and 'spade' sound like bridge, where to ruff is to trump; but a ruff is also a wading bird. EVER turned round holds the E.
explanation.definitionFit: The ruff is a sandpiper whose female is called a reeve, so she is the male bird's mate.

clue.text: Like one of those 24 hour bugs?

definitions.text: Like one of those 24 hour bugs?

blocks.note: surface reading: a stomach bug or virus that lasts only a day
setter's reading: the bugs are insects, mayflies, whose adult life lasts about a day, and the answer is the adjective for things that brief

explanation.surface: Someone describes an illness as one of those short-lived bugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bugs' suggests an illness; it means the mayfly, whose scientific order Ephemeroptera gives the word its sense of a one-day life.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes anything that lasts a very short time, originally a single day, as a mayfly does.
